general.temas: The final stretch of the election campaign dominates several front pages, with attention on opinion polls, voter turnout and the debate between Sánchez and Feijóo. The support for Sánchez from former ministers under Felipe González and sports news about Alcaraz and Márquez also feature repeatedly. Only OKdiario highlights the work to move the A-5 underground in Madrid.
general.motivo_crispacion: The campaign features numerous verbal clashes: Feijóo warns about Sánchez, while Sánchez describes the PP and Vox as a step backwards. There are also recriminations between parties with similar positions, such as Abascal’s criticism of the PP and the Broad Front’s criticism of the PSOE. Warnings about rights, the Constitution and immigration add to the tension, as do some headlines using polarizing language. These are offset by sports, cultural and service news, particularly in ABC, El Mundo and OKdiario.

El País.resumen:
- Polls show a narrowing gap between the PP and the PSOE and a decline for Vox.
- The front page brings together polling averages, interviews and analysis of voting by region and province.
- Former members of Felipe González’s government call for a vote for Sánchez and warn of a risk of regression.
- Feijóo, Sánchez and Colau headline campaign events and call on their supporters to turn out.
- Two analyses examine Sánchez’s approach and Feijóo’s preparations for the debate.
El País.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although some quotations and expressions resort to alarm and confrontation, such as “they are capable of anything,” “he will demolish the Constitution” and “wipe the smile off Feijóo’s face.”
El País.sesgo: The selection focuses on the electoral contest and includes voices from different parties, with prominent attention to left-wing options and support for Sánchez from former Socialist leaders. The analyses of the debate use evaluative terms such as “lack of conviction” and “triumphalism.”

El Mundo.resumen:
- Feijóo calls for voter mobilization in Valencia and Abascal criticizes the PP and tactical voting.
- Sánchez makes spending pledges and announces an extension of the bank tax; former ministers under González call for a vote for the PSOE.
- Yolanda Díaz criticizes the Socialist strategy, while Aznar and Ayuso urge people to vote to replace Sánchez.
- Alcaraz reaches the ATP Finals final, Márquez crashes close to clinching the title and Nadal joins Real Madrid’s board.
- The Plan Auto+ runs out of funds; cyberattacks against US agencies are reported.
El Mundo.motivo_populismo: The front page combines information with expressions of confrontation and alarm such as “they are capable of anything,” “a step backwards” and “Spain is going to commit suicide as a nation,” although they are attributed to the politicians quoted.
El Mundo.sesgo: The selection prioritizes the election campaign and clashes between leaders, with several political forces represented. It also gives prominence to sport; no conclusive partisan leaning can be discerned from these headlines alone.

ABC.resumen:
- Gianni de Gennaro, the former Italian police chief under investigation over the attack on Borsellino, is found dead.
- Alcaraz reaches his second consecutive ATP Finals final and Márquez crashes close to securing his tenth world title.
- A child is hospitalized in Valencia after falling from a first-floor window and the Civil Guard dismantles a group growing and selling marijuana in Rivas.
- The front page carries comments on the debate between Sánchez and Feijóo and a political opinion article, as well as a story about the relationship between the United Kingdom and the EU.
- It also covers food, theater, music and the appointment of Aurelio García Macías as personal archbishop.
ABC.motivo_populismo: Most of the headlines are informative, although expressions such as “flooded with drugs” and “has crushed him” resort to drama and confrontational language.
ABC.sesgo: The selection combines crime and other incidents, sport, politics and culture, with attention to local news. Political coverage includes confrontational approaches and differing opinions on the debate, but no uniform leaning can be inferred across the entire front page.

Público.resumen:
- As the campaign closes, the PSOE is gaining ground, but lacks a majority to govern against the PP and Vox.
- Irene Montero criticizes the PSOE’s appeal for tactical voting, and former members of Felipe González’s government call for a vote for Sánchez.
- Several headlines question Feijóo and warn about Vox and the future of euthanasia.
- An initiative seeks to give a voice to people without the right to vote, and the influence of regional nationalist parties in Congress is examined.
- The campaign also sparks debate in the Church; another piece looks at Pepa Millán and memetics.
Público.motivo_populismo: Alarmist or disparaging expressions stand out, such as “psychopaths,” “disguise himself as a manager” and the risk of losing a right, although several headlines maintain an informative tone.
Público.sesgo: The selection and wording show an approach closer to progressive positions, with particularly critical attention to the PP and Vox. It also includes criticism of the PSOE by Irene Montero.

OKdiario.resumen:
- Madrid is working to connect the A-5 and M-30 tunnels before the opening scheduled for December 23.
- The president of the El Hierro Island Council travels to Venezuela to meet residents of the island, while protests against illegal immigration are taking place there.
- Plus Ultra is reportedly set to close its last scheduled route, to Venezuela, affecting 35,000 passengers, according to sources close to the company.
- MotoGP accounts for part of the sports coverage, with Márquez’s crash and Martín’s title chances; it also includes a complaint by Arbeloa about refereeing.
- The front page includes content on psychology and literature, quotations from public figures and advice on pests and home insulation.
OKdiario.motivo_populismo: Accusatory or emotional formulations such as “abandons his neighbors” and “leaves them stranded” stand out, alongside headlines that present advice as certainty; others maintain an informative tone.
OKdiario.sesgo: The political coverage presents the Island Council president’s trip as an abandonment of local residents and contrasts the pursuit of votes with protests against illegal immigration. The Plus Ultra story highlights its bailout with public money and links it to Pedro Sánchez’s government.

opiniones.comunista:
I do not want the campaign reduced to who won a debate or which party benefits from tactical voting. The decisive question is who controls the wealth we produce and whose interests the next government will serve.

The promise of more spending on healthcare, education and housing must translate into universal public services and housing outside the logic of speculation. The extension of the bank tax is welcome, but taxing their profits is not enough: I advocate a democratically controlled public banking system that puts credit at the service of collective needs. I also support a shorter working week with no loss of pay.

In the face of big capital, the working class needs organization and collective ownership, not just election promises. And that class includes migrants: their rights cannot depend on their economic usefulness or become campaign bargaining chips.
opiniones.anarquista:
I see a campaign that has turned into a competition to consolidate votes and manage fear. Polls and seat projections matter, but they should not reduce our political life to choosing who is in charge. I distrust both the state and the parties that aspire to run it: delegating power does not eliminate hierarchies, it reproduces them.

Spending promises on healthcare, education and housing point to real needs; it is not enough to wait for a government to decide how to meet them. I believe that those who work in and use those services should be able to organize and control them directly, through open assemblies and coordination between communities. The initiative seeking to give a voice to those excluded from the ballot box also reminds us that living in a society and being able to make decisions about it do not always go hand in hand. For me, freedom requires mutual aid, equality and participation by everyone affected.
opiniones.liberal:
I see a campaign too focused on who wins the debate and too little on how much power the next government will have over our decisions. The promise to increase spending on healthcare, education and housing deserves a simple question: who will pay the bill, and with what results? A percentage does not guarantee better services.

The extension of the bank tax also gives us reason to distrust exceptional taxes that are prolonged. Their cost may ultimately be passed on to customers and savers. I prefer low taxes, stable rules and competition, not a state that makes more and more decisions for us.

I also question subsidies for electric cars: spending public money to favor one technology takes resources away from other priorities and leaves taxpayers bearing the costs of decisions that consumers and businesses should make on their own responsibility.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I see a campaign bent on turning the vote into an arithmetic exercise. Polls, averages and calls for tactical voting take center stage, while essential questions are pushed aside: who decides what happens at our borders, how we protect our families and what traditions we want to pass on.

The prime minister emphasizes migrants’ contribution to Spanish prosperity. I do not deny it, but a sovereign nation has a duty to strictly control who enters and remains on its territory. This is not a matter of hostility, but of security, enforcement of the law and capacity for integration.

Nor is it enough for me that the PP celebrates a good debate performance or holds a large rally. I want clear commitments, not an advance allocation of ministries. And I distrust political and media elites who ask us to choose between campaign slogans instead of discussing Spain’s direction.
opiniones.centro:
I am concerned about a campaign in which polls and warnings about opponents seem to take up more space than potential agreements. Mobilization is legitimate, but presenting every election as an existential threat makes it harder, once the votes are cast, for representatives to recognize one another as legitimate counterparts and for institutions to function.

Promises of more resources for healthcare, education and housing deserve a serious debate about financing, priorities and results. The extension of the bank tax also requires an assessment of its effects, not just the revenue it raises: we need strong public services and a predictable environment for investment. I prefer gradual, negotiated reforms whose results can be assessed to big announcements without adequate explanation. And I agree on the need to recognize migrants’ contribution, without abandoning a rigorous debate on how to manage immigration.
